                                      PROJECT NO. 58777

 TRIENNIAL RELIABILITY                           §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION

                ELECTRIC RELIABILITY COUNCIL OF TEXAS, INC.S
               REPORT ON 2026 RELIABILITY STANDARD MAGNITUDE

         Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (ERCOT) provides this Report on 2026
Reliability Standard Magnitude. Pursuant to the requirement in 16 Texas Administrative Code
(TAC) § 25.508(b)(3), this report is timely filed by December 1, 2025. A table summarizing
Transmission Operators (TOs) responses to ERCOTs Request for Information (RFI) is included
as Attachment A and TOs complete responses to the RFI are included as Attachments B1
through B26.

                                      I.      BACKGROUND
         The reliability standard established by the Public Utility Commission of Texas
(Commission) in 16 TAC § 25.508 consists of three criteria: frequency, duration, and magnitude
of a loss of load event as reflected in modeled simulations. Values for the frequency and duration
criteria are established by the rule. For the magnitude criterion, § 25.508(b)(3) requires:

         (3)   Magnitude. The expected highest level of load shed during a loss of load
               event for the ERCOT region, measured as the average lost load for a given
               hour, must be less than the maximum number of megawatts of load shed
               that can be safely rotated during a loss of load event, as determined by
               ERCOT, in consultation with commission staff and the transmission
               operators, with a 1.00 percent exceedance tolerance. Beginning in 2024, on
               or before December 1 of each year, ERCOT must file the maximum number
               of megawatts of load shed that can be safely rotated during a loss of load
               event and a summary of the methodology used to calculate this value.

Accordingly, the value for the magnitude criterion must be determined on an annual basis by
ERCOT in consultation with Commission Staff and the TOs.
         The 2025 magnitude was the first magnitude determination, which is 16,000 megawatts
(MW) with a one percent exceedance tolerance. To inform the determination of that magnitude,
in fall 2024 ERCOT issued two sets of Requests for Information (RFIs) to TOs to gather data on
the total amount of load that could be included in load shed rotation programs and, of that total
load included in load shed rotation programs, the amount of load that could be safely shed at any

 one time to facilitate rotation of the load shed. The RFIs related to winter 2024-2025 were based
on a forecasted total load for the ERCOT Region of 80,000 MW, which used the 75th percentile
load forecast with limited adjustments. After holding a series of consultations with TOs and
Commission Staff, on February 6, 2025, ERCOT filed its report proposing a methodology to
determine the magnitude of 20% of the forecasted winter peak load using approximately the 75th
percentile load forecast. As explained in the report, ERCOT recommended that the TOs RFI
responses provided sufficient support to justify a magnitude of 16,000 MW that would result from
that methodology.1 On February 7, 2025, Commission Staff filed a memorandum agreeing that
the proposed methodology and magnitude value were reasonable.2 At the Open Meeting on
February 13, 2025, the Commission indicated agreement with this approach and the magnitude
value.

                           II.      2026 MAGNITUDE DEVELOPMENT PROCESS

A.       Consultation Process
         To determine the magnitude development methodology for the 2026 value, ERCOT began
consulting with Commission Staff in late September 2025 and had an initial consultation call with
Commission Staff on October 1, 2025, to discuss issuing a magnitude-related Request for
Information (RFI) to the Transmission Operators (TOs). The RFI questions being considered were
based on the 2025 RFI questions but significantly more streamlined.                          After incorporating
Commission Staffs feedback, ERCOT issued the RFI to TOs on October 7, 2025, and also posted
to the ERCOT website the load forecast for winter 2025-2026 that is used in the RFIs.3 To provide
transparency to stakeholders, ERCOT issued a Market Notice that included the generic version of
the RFI to TOs and publicized the posting of the load forecast to the ERCOT website.4
         On October 9, 2025, ERCOT hosted a consultation call with the TOs and Commission
Staff. The agenda of that consultation included a refresher on the reliability standard rule and how

determine the 2026 magnitude and an opportunity for questions about the newly issued RFIs.
         Responses to the RFIs were largely provided by October 24, 2025. ERCOT circulated the
package of TO RFI responses to Commission Staff and all of the TOs and then hosted a second
general consultation call on November 4, 2025, to review and discuss the results. During this
consultation call, ERCOT confirmed that the aggregated responses to the RFI would be reported
to the Commission for use as the 2026 magnitude value. After the consultation, ERCOT received
revised RFI responses from certain TOs and ERCOT circulated the revised package of RFI
responses to all TOs and Commission Staff.

B.       RFI Development
         As noted previously, the 2026 magnitude RFIs were based on the 2025 RFIs by using the
same question structure and base load forecast approach. Each RFI begins with a statement of the
forecasted ERCOT System peak load for winter 2025-2026, the TOs forecasted share of that
System peak load, and instructs the TO to assume that the expected duration of the loss of load
event is one hour. This load forecast starts with the base economic forecast, adds forecasted load
for electric vehicle (EV) charging load and large flexible loads (LFL), and subtracts behind-the-
meter solar generation. The 2025 RFIs used an adjusted 75th percentile winter load forecast and
accordingly the 2026 RFIs also use the 75th percentile winter load forecast, albeit with application
of the ERCOT adjustment methodology that was developed in 2025.5 This resulted in a total
ERCOT System winter 2025-2026 peak load of 77,338 MW.
         The RFI instructions explain that the 77,338 MW does not include any Large Load MW
subject to curtailment under Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §§ 37.0561(e) and 39.169.
Those provisions of PURA were established by Senate Bill (S.B.) 6:6 § 37.0561(e) establishes
curtailment requirements for large loads that have at least 50% on-site backup generation and
§ 39.169 establishes curtailment requirements for large loads that are co-located with certain
generators. These are only two of the large load curtailment provisions established by S.B. 6,

see also generally, Reports of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Project No. 55999, ERCOTs Revisions to
Adjusted Load Forecasts and Amended Draft Proposed Order (June 4, 2025) (describing the methodology for the
ERCOT Adjusted Load Forecast and the ERCOT Transmission Planning Adjusted Load Forecast).

 however those are the two S.B. 6 requirements that are in place and will affect large loads that
come in service by the January 31, 2026. This is the date of the forecasted ERCOT System winter
peak. To calculate the 77,338 MW, 3,309 MW of contracted large loads and 1,508 MW of officer-
letter large loads that are not currently on the system but are projected to be in service by January
31, 2026, were subtracted from the total 82,155 MW load forecast for the ERCOT System at its
winter peak. For informational purposes, RFI No. 1-3 was included to request that each TO then
quantify the total amount of large load MW that is subject to either of those S.B. 6 provisions and
is anticipated to be in service by January 31, 2026. That is load that would be anticipated to be
shed prior to activation of the load shed rotation programs referenced in RFI Nos. 1-1 and 1-2.
         RFI No. 1-1 requests that each TO state the maximum MW of load from that winter peak
load amount that the TO can include in a load shed rotation program to be used during a loss of
load event. Because the focus of the magnitude criterion is on the maximum MW of load shed
that can be rotated, RFI No. 1-2 then requests the maximum MW from the TOs program that can
be safely shed at any one time to facilitate rotation. For example, if a TO serves a total of 200
MW of load and from that total includes 100 MW in its load shed rotation program with a target
rotation of 50%, then the amount of load the TO would shed at any one time to facilitate rotation
would be 50 MW. Note that not all TOs target a 50% rotation, so each TOs response to RFI No.
1-2 is not necessarily half of the total program load from RFI No. 1-1.7
         The 2025 RFIs included additional questions that were not included in the 2026 RFIs. This
was largely because the 2025 RFIs were the initial instance of the magnitude development and
ERCOT cast a broad net to determine what kind of information could be ascertained from the RFIs.
After receiving the TOs responses to those 2025 RFIs, it became clear that certain questions did
not provide sufficient value. For instance, the 2025 RFIs asked for data on expected loss of load
event durations of one, four, and twelve hours to determine if there was a difference in TOs ability
to shed load as a loss of load event progresses. The differences between the responses provided
for each of these scenarios were not as significant as anticipated and therefore did not appear to
justify asking similar questions this year. The 2025 RFIs also requested information for loss of
load event scenarios in a future year in order to determine if TOs anticipated being able to rotate
additional MW due to further system segmentation or other technology changes. However, most

 TOs did not address impacts of projected technology or segmentation changes in their RFI
responses and instead simply scaled their response by the same amount as the increase to the future
ERCOT System load. For this reason, there did not appear to be additional insights to be gleaned
from including such RFI questions. Finally, the 2025 RFIs requested that TOs exclude certain
categories of load (i.e., load associated with Under-Frequency Load Shed (UFLS) and non-
residential critical loads) from their load shed rotation program responses. This was done in an
attempt to standardize TO responses based on ascribing a shared meaning to the rules reference
to load shed that can be safely rotated during a loss of load event.8 However, it became clear
that in reality TO practices varied widely as to what loads each considered could be safely rotated.
To avoid arbitrarily constraining the loads that each TO could respond to the RFIs with, ERCOT
did not include such broad-based limitations in the 2026 magnitude RFIs.

                     III.     2026 MAGNITUDE METHODOLOGY RECOMMENDATION
         After considering the data provided in TOs RFI responses and the feedback of TOs and
Commission Staff during the consultations, ERCOT recommends that the methodology to
determine the value of the magnitude criterion for the 2026 value be to aggregate TO responses to
ERCOT RFI No. 1-2. Use of the aggregated response to this RFI best reflects TOs indicated
capabilities for the purposes of establishing a systemwide magnitude for the ERCOT Region.9 The
one percent exceedance tolerance would then be applied to that value.

                                    IV.      MAGNITUDE VALUE FOR 2026
         By aggregating TO responses to RFI No. 1-2, this would result in a magnitude value of
13,988 MW for 2026 plus a one percent exceedance tolerance. Based on a winter ERCOT System
peak load of 77,338 MW as the ERCOT-adjusted 75th percentile forecast, TOs stated in response

           As noted in ERCOTs filing of the 2025 magnitude, Commission Staffs responsive memorandum, and the
Commissions subsequent discussion at the February 13, 2025, Open Meeting, it is important to emphasize that the
magnitude is not a performance standard for TOs during real-time load shed events nor does the magnitude
methodology proposed herein direct TOs how to structure their load shed plans. See, Reports of the Electric Reliability
Council of Texas, Project No. 55999, ERCOTs Report on Reliability Standard Magnitude Methodology at 8 (Feb. 6,
2025); see also, Reports of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Project No. 55999, Commission Staff
Memorandum on ERCOTs Report on Reliability Standard Magnitude Methodology at 2-3 (Feb. 7, 2025). A TOs
performance during a real-time load shed event will be measured by its compliance with the directives issued by
ERCOT Operators and TOs continue to have responsibility for, and discretion over, the development and
implementation of their own individualized load shed plans. The magnitude value sets a capabilities expectation that
factors into the evaluation of the level of systemwide reliability for the ERCOT Region.

 to RFI No. 1-2 that 13,988 MW is the systemwide amount of load from their aggregated load shed
rotation programs that could be safely shed at any one time to facilitate load shed rotation.
         Pursuant to 16 TAC § 25.508(c), ERCOT is required to conduct a reliability assessment at
least once every three years beginning on January 1, 2026, to determine whether the bulk power
system for the ERCOT Region is currently meeting the reliability standard and is likely to continue
to meet the standard for the subsequent three years. Note that it will not be known whether any
magnitude value would make that the binding criterion of the reliability standard until ERCOT has
performed the modeling for the reliability assessment in 2026.             Furthermore, 16 TAC
§ 25.508(c)(1)(A) requires ERCOT to file a comprehensive list of proposed modeling assumptions
with the Commission to be used in the reliability assessment. The Commission will then provide
stakeholders with at least 30 days to file comments on ERCOTs proposed modeling assumptions.
ERCOT intends to include the 2026 magnitude value in its filing of assumptions for stakeholder
comment. Therefore, unlike most years in which only TOs and Commission Staff provide
feedback on the development of the magnitude value, all stakeholders will have the opportunity to
provide feedback on the appropriate magnitude in years in which the reliability assessment is
performed.

                                       V.     CONCLUSION
         ERCOT would like to thank the TOs and Commission Staff for their time and support in
consulting throughout this second iteration of the magnitude methodology development process.
ERCOT appreciates the Commissions consideration of this report and would be pleased to provide
any additional information. ERCOT personnel will attend the Commissions December 12 or 18,
2025 Open Meeting, depending on the Commissions preference, to be available for questions and
feedback.

                                      I.      BACKGROUND
         The reliability standard established by the Public Utility Commission of Texas
(Commission) in 16 TAC § 25.508 consists of three criteria: frequency, duration, and magnitude
of a loss of load event as reflected in modeled simulations. Values for the frequency and duration
criteria are established by the rule. For the magnitude criterion, § 25.508(b)(3) requires:

         (3)   Magnitude. The expected highest level of load shed during a loss of load
               event for the ERCOT region, measured as the average lost load for a given
               hour, must be less than the maximum number of megawatts of load shed
               that can be safely rotated during a loss of load event, as determined by
               ERCOT, in consultation with commission staff and the transmission
               operators, with a 1.00 percent exceedance tolerance. Beginning in 2024, on
               or before December 1 of each year, ERCOT must file the maximum number
               of megawatts of load shed that can be safely rotated during a loss of load
               event and a summary of the methodology used to calculate this value.

Accordingly, the value for the magnitude criterion must be determined on an annual basis by
ERCOT in consultation with Commission Staff and the TOs.
         The 2025 magnitude was the first magnitude determination, which is 16,000 megawatts
(MW) with a one percent exceedance tolerance. To inform the determination of that magnitude,
in fall 2024 ERCOT issued two sets of Requests for Information (RFIs) to TOs to gather data on
the total amount of load that could be included in load shed rotation programs and, of that total
load included in load shed rotation programs, the amount of load that could be safely shed at any
